name: Zane Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a longwall cutting shift at a large coal mine and run the shearer when the seam bends. That's the machine that slices coal from a long face, with roof supports moving behind it. A two-year technical diploma got me onto the crew, and years of spotting weak roof taught me when to stop. My partner Ruth works at a library, our children are grown, and we have about four months of expenses saved. We still owe a little on the house and hope I can retire at 65. I don't use AI tools; the shift log and the crew's eyes suit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a faster shift log is fine if it doesn't replace a roof inspection. The shearer still needs someone close enough to hear a cutting head bind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our regular pay and Ruth's library wage will carry on. Four months saved is not a fortune, but with the house loan nearly finished I can sleep in this mild picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the roof check with the apprentices before the shearer starts. In the first year I'll put the same amount into our house loan each pay day and ask the electrician to verify any computer-drafted fault note before I sign it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about my job and our bills. I don't want a smooth form to turn a weak roof into somebody else's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a roof check change the shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter a support leg sank a little after a wet seam opened, so I stopped the cutting head. The crew moved the support before another pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your house payments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ruth the house payment stays as planned and the library income can remain for ordinary bills. I would not make our grown children worry over a faster form.

say: I would accept a **faster log** while keeping a real roof inspection.
I would tell the crew the **cutting head** still needs a nearby operator.
think: I expect **regular pay** and Ruth’s library income to continue.
I think our **four-month cushion** and nearly finished house loan make this picture manageable.
do: **Keep checking** roof supports with apprentices before the shearer starts.
**Ask the electrician** to verify computer-drafted fault notes before I sign them.
**Maintain** the scheduled house-loan payment from each payday.
feel: **Steady** about pay, with concern that neat forms might hide weak ground.
S0.quote: The shearer still needs someone close enough to hear a cutting head bind.
fieldNote: His **roof judgment** comes from a sinking support leg and direct checks before cutting.
The **four-month cushion**, regular mine pay and library wage support a calm response to modest paperwork change.

steps.text: Keep checking roof supports with apprentices before cutting
Ask the electrician to verify computer-drafted faults before signing
Make scheduled house-loan payments each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the planning office may change before a robot can work the coal face. I want the union safety committee to see new cutting targets before managers press them onto a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think faster plans could mean fewer pauses for roof checks and a harder night for the newest worker. My lead pay should hold, but I would not trade a support inspection for another row of coal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll take our last four shift logs to the union safety committee and ask them to compare planned metres with roof stops. In the first year I'll record every time the new schedule tries to shorten a support check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy for the crew, not frightened for our own groceries. A target on paper can become pressure from a supervisor underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you stop a new cutting plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a plan shows the next pass before a loose support is secured, I will stop the shearer. The roof does not read the production target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprentice record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the apprentice to mark the support number in the log while I call the supervisor. That gives the committee a record they can use.

say: I would expect **office planning** to change before robots reach the coal face.
I would ask the **union committee** to review cutting targets before shifts follow them.
think: I expect my **lead pay** to hold, though faster plans may squeeze roof checks.
I worry the **newest worker** will face pressure to rush a support inspection.
do: **Bring four logs** to the union safety committee for a comparison of targets and stops.
**Record shortened checks** during the first year of any new cutting schedule.
feel: **Uneasy** for crew safety while his own household income feels secure.
S1.quote: The roof does not read the production target.
fieldNote: He treats **thinking-task planning** as the early change and asks for a record of lost safety time.
His **union action** protects roof checks; he does not describe immediate loss of his own pay.

steps.text: Bring four shift logs to the union safety committee
Keep recording roof checks against any new cutting schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 could write plans, while capable shearer robots follow around 2031. The mine should bargain a paid bridge for workers who are close to retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots arrive, two years before I hope to retire. Four months saved and a house loan still due would not carry us through a long break in mine wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union to negotiate two years of paid bridge work or pension contributions for operators nearing 65. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll stay on the cutting shift while it exists and apply for a posted roof-check job only if the pay covers our house payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing two earning years, though I have people to bargain with and some nearby mines to ask. My partner's library wage cannot carry our whole house loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which purchase would wait at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Ruth we should postpone replacing the car until we know what the mine will pay. A working car can last another winter if the brakes are sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a roof-check post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the safety lead whether a roof-check post has paid shifts, not just a new title. I won't leave a typical mine wage for a promise on a notice board.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AI** from capable shearer robots around 2031.
I would seek a **paid retirement bridge** for operators losing final working years.
think: I think at **63**, I could lose two years of mine wages before planned retirement.
I think our **four months saved** and remaining house loan make a long break unaffordable.
do: **Ask the union** for paid bridge work or pension contributions this year.
**Keep** cutting shifts; apply for a posted roof-check job only if its pay covers the house payment.
**Postpone car replacement** until the mine states what it will pay.
feel: **Anxious** about two lost earning years, with bargaining and nearby work as possible routes.
S2.quote: My partner's library wage cannot carry our whole house loan.
fieldNote: His **2031 age** is 63, and the robot date could cost two final years of wages.
The **roof-check application** needs a posted job and house-covering pay; he will not count a vague bridge promise.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate bridge work or pension contributions
Apply for a posted roof-check job if pay covers the house payment
Postpone car replacement until mine bridge pay is clear
Keep operating the cutting shift while human work remains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 might change plans, while capable shearer robots come around 2034. I would be 66 then, so the robot date falls after the age I hope to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still need the mine wage until 65 and a pension that covers the house and bills. Our four-month cushion could cover a short mine pay gap, but I would not retire on a pension estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the retirement office this year for figures at 65 and 67, then keep leading the cutting shift if my health holds. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll set a retirement date only if the written pension covers the house payment and usual bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly calm about the robot date, but the pension amount must be real. Extra years to prepare only help when the mine keeps paying us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension is below the estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a written pension figure at 65 is too low, I would ask about one more year on the cutting crew. I would take a posted nearby mine job only if this mine ends my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you tell your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown son the date once Ruth and I have checked the numbers together. I won't ask him to pay off the house just so I can retire on time.

say: I would note **2034 robots** arrive after my hoped-for retirement at 65.
I would demand **written pension figures** before setting a date.
think: I still need **mine wages** until 65 and a pension covering the house.
I think our **four-month cushion** bridges a short gap, not an unknown pension shortfall.
do: **Request pension figures** for ages 65 and 67 this year.
**Keep leading** the cutting crew if healthy and set retirement only when written pension covers bills.
feel: **Mostly calm** about robot timing, while needing certainty about pension income.
S3.quote: Our four-month cushion could cover a short mine pay gap, but I would not retire on a pension estimate.
fieldNote: His **2034 age** is 66, one year after hoped-for retirement.
He keeps **retirement conditional** on a written pension covering house and bills and continued safe work until then.

steps.text: Request written pension figures for ages 65 and 67
Keep leading cutting shifts if healthy until pension covers house and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 and capable shearer robots around 2039 come after my hoped-for retirement. I want the union to secure younger operators' paid apprenticeships while there is time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 when robots come, if I live to see both dates. I expect to be retired by then if the pension covers our bills, but a four-month reserve alone cannot carry two people for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working safely and paying the house loan on schedule while the shifts last. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, if retired as planned, I'll review the pension budget with Ruth and speak at a union meeting about paid apprenticeships for younger workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the robot timing for myself. I would be disappointed if the mine used ten years of warning to offer younger workers only an unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension does not cover bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our pension comes in below the bills, I would ask for another posted mine shift nearby before using the reserve. I would need an actual offer, not a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell apprentices before leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell apprentices to learn roof supports from the crew before learning a new screen. A mine safety certificate means more when a skilled worker can watch you make the stop call.

say: I would expect **2039 shearer robots** after my planned retirement.
I would press for **paid apprenticeships** for younger operators during the decade.
think: I think at **68 and 71**, I expect retirement if the pension covers normal bills.
I think our **four-month reserve** cannot support an indefinite retirement without pension income.
do: **Keep working** safely and paying the house loan while shifts last.
**Review pension bills** with Ruth after thinking AI arrives if retired as planned.
**Speak for paid apprenticeships** at a union meeting after thinking AI arrives.
feel: **Calm** about his own robot timing and concerned for younger workers’ training terms.
S4.quote: A mine safety certificate means more when a skilled worker can watch you make the stop call.
fieldNote: His **2036 and 2039 ages** are 68 and 71, beyond planned retirement.
He pairs **conditional pension security** with union support for paid apprenticeships, rather than learning AI himself.

steps.text: Keep leading safe cutting shifts and paying the house loan
Review pension income against bills with Ruth after 2036 if retired
Speak for paid apprenticeships at a union meeting after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable shearer robots could reach the mine around 2031, two years before I hope to retire. A negotiated paid bridge or a posted roof-check job at house-covering pay would help Ruth and me keep our plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I trust a robot to spot a loose support. I do not, and The apprentice who sees a mine roof support move must have the power to stop the cutting line. I would want that right written into the shift rules.

headlineQuote: The apprentice who sees a mine roof support move must have the power to stop the cutting line.
portrait: **Zane Costa**, 58, leads longwall cutting at a large coal mine and has a two-year technical diploma.
He has **typical mine pay**, four months of savings and a nearly finished house loan alongside his partner’s library wage.
He avoids **AI tools** and relies on roof checks, shift logs and union safety meetings.
He hopes to **retire at 65**, making 2031 robots at 63 a risk to two final earning years.
His **job move** depends on a posted roof-check role with pay sufficient for the house, while later dates depend on pension figures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable shearer robots could arrive two years before planned retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **negotiated paid bridge** or posted roof-check work with enough pay for the house would help.
